config.title: Test Context

intro.title: Test Context
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that uses the Context API to manage and share a theme (like 'light' or 'dark') across different parts of your application without passing props manually. You'll learn how to create a context, provide its value from a parent component, and consume it in a child component using the useContext hook. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript for type safety, and the Context API for state management. By the end, you'll understand how context helps avoid 'prop drilling' and makes your components cleaner and more maintainable.
intro.usecase: Testing React Context is essential for building complex applications where state needs to be shared across multiple components, such as user authentication systems, theme switchers, or shopping carts. In real products, this pattern appears in dashboards where user preferences persist across panels, e-commerce sites managing cart state across pages, or apps with dark/light mode toggles. Developers must test Context to ensure components correctly consume and update shared state, preventing bugs like incorrect user sessions or broken theme persistence. This ensures reliable behavior in interactive UIs like multi-step forms, real-time notifications, or collaborative tools where state consistency is critical.

objectives: Apply the useContext hook to access context values within functional components.
Implement a Context Provider component to wrap and supply data to child components.
Construct a Context object using React.createContext with appropriate TypeScript typing.
Define a default value for the Context to handle cases where components are used outside a Provider.
Utilize the Provider's value prop to pass data and functions down the component tree.
Control component rendering by consuming context values to conditionally display elements.
Execute context updates by passing state setters through the Provider to modify shared data.
Access multiple contexts within a single component by nesting multiple useContext calls.
Modify component behavior by using context values to determine styling, content, or functionality.
Store and retrieve shared application state (like theme, user data, or preferences) using Context.
Handle context consumption in deeply nested components without prop drilling.
Compare context usage versus prop passing for managing shared state across components.

steps.title: Import React and createContext from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the createContext function from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and createContext from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and createContext
import React, { createContext } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and createContext from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported, making React and createContext available for use in the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and createContext. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the ability to create context objects.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import statement. Make sure you're importing both React and createContext from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires importing React and createContext from the 'react' package. Look at the example and try again.

steps.title: Define the context type interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'TestContextType' that describes the shape of the context value. It should have a 'message' property of type 'string' and a 'count' property of type 'number'.
steps.hint: Create an interface using the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and its property definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a TypeScript interface named 'TestContextType' with the required properties, ready to be used for typing the context value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the TestContextType interface with the correct property types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface includes both required properties with the correct TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to use the 'interface' keyword, name it 'TestContextType', and include both 'message: string' and 'count: number' properties.

steps.title: Create a context with default values
steps.instruction: Create a context using createContext with default values that match the TestContextType interface. Use the name TestContext for your context variable.
steps.hint: Call createContext with an object containing the default values for your context. Make sure the object structure matches your TestContextType interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TestContext variable created with createContext, initialized with default values that match the TestContextType interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully created a context with default values that match the interface. This context will provide the initial state for components that consume it.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with the default values or context creation. Make sure you're calling createContext with an object that has both isActive and toggleActive properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The context wasn't created correctly. You need to call createContext with default values that match the TestContextType interface structure.

steps.title: Create a provider component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TestContextProvider that accepts children as props. Use the React.FC type with a props interface that includes children: React.ReactNode.
steps.hint: Define a component that will wrap other components and provide the context value. Start with either 'function TestContextProvider(props: Props)' or 'const TestContextProvider: React.FC<Props> = (props) =>'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TestContextProvider component is defined with proper TypeScript typing for children props.
successCriteria: The component should be named TestContextProvider, accept children as props with type React.ReactNode, and return JSX (you can return a fragment or div for now).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the provider component with proper TypeScript typing for children.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component accepts children as props with the correct type (React.ReactNode) and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The provider component is missing or incorrect. Create a component named TestContextProvider that accepts children as props and returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize state in the provider
steps.instruction: Inside the provider component, add a useState hook to manage a boolean state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook from React. Remember to import it if needed, but it's already imported from 'react' in step 1.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The provider component will have a state variable 'isActive' initialized to false, ready to be used in the context value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isActive state variable with useState. This state will be used to track the active status in your context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a boolean state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a useState hook inside the provider component to create a boolean state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Define context value object
steps.instruction: Inside your provider component, create a value object that contains the isActive state and toggleActive function. This object should match the TestContextType interface.
steps.hint: Create a variable called 'value' that is an object with properties isActive and toggleActive.
steps.expectedOutcome: A value object is created that will be passed to the context provider.
successCriteria: The code should contain a value object with isActive and toggleActive properties that match the TestContextType interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the context value object. This object contains the state and function that will be provided to all components consuming this context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the value object needs both isActive and toggleActive properties. Make sure toggleActive is a function that will eventually toggle the isActive state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The value object is missing or doesn't match the required structure. Create an object with isActive and toggleActive properties that align with the TestContextType interface.

steps.title: Return the Provider with value
steps.instruction: In your provider component, return the Provider component with the value prop set to the context value object you defined.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax to return the Provider component with the value prop.
steps.expectedOutcome: The provider component now returns the Provider JSX element with the value prop properly set.
successCriteria: The provider component returns a JSX element containing the Provider component with the value prop set to the context value object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the Provider component with the value prop. This makes the context value available to all child components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning the Provider component with the value prop set to the context value object. Check your JSX syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The provider component needs to return the Provider component with the value prop. Review how to return JSX elements and set props.

steps.title: Create a consumer component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TestConsumer that will consume and display the context values. The component should return JSX.
steps.hint: Define a new component using either function declaration or arrow function syntax. For now, just create the component structure without implementing the context consumption logic.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new TestConsumer component is defined with a basic structure that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the TestConsumer component. This component will serve as the consumer of your context values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a component named 'TestConsumer' that returns JSX. Check that the component name is spelled correctly and includes a return statement with JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TestConsumer component isn't properly defined. Make sure you create a functional component named 'TestConsumer' that returns JSX (like a div or fragment).

steps.title: Use useContext to access context
steps.instruction: Inside the TestConsumer component, use the useContext hook to access the TestContext values.
steps.hint: Call useContext with the TestContext as its argument to get the context value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TestConsumer component now has access to the context values via useContext.
successCriteria: TestContext is passed as the argument to useContext
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used useContext to access the context values in the consumer component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useContext with TestContext as its argument inside the TestConsumer component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TestConsumer component should use useContext to access the TestContext values. Try calling useContext(TestContext) inside the component.

steps.title: Display context values in JSX
steps.instruction: Inside the TestConsumer component, display the current isActive value from context in the JSX. Add a paragraph element that shows the isActive state.
steps.hint: Access the context value you destructured earlier and use it in JSX with curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TestConsumer component will show the current isActive value from context in the UI.
successCriteria: The TestConsumer component should display the isActive value from context in a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the context value in your component's JSX. This shows how context data can be rendered in the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're actually displaying the isActive value from context in the JSX. Check that you're using curly braces to embed the value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The isActive value from context isn't being displayed in the JSX. Remember to access the context value and use it within a paragraph element.

steps.title: Add update buttons and wire onClick handlers
steps.instruction: In the TestConsumer component, add a button that calls toggleActive from the context when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the toggleActive function from the context value as the onClick handler for a button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TestConsumer component will include a button that, when clicked, triggers the toggleActive function from the context.
successCriteria: The button element must have an onClick attribute set to toggleActive from the context.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that calls the toggleActive function when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the button's onClick is set to toggleActive from the context.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or its onClick handler is not correctly wired to toggleActive.

steps.title: Wrap the app with the provider
steps.instruction: Wrap the main app component with the TestProvider to make the context available to the entire application.
steps.hint: In your main App component, wrap the content with <TestProvider> tags.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TestProvider wraps the main App component, making the context available to all child components.
successCriteria: The App component is wrapped with <TestProvider>
The TestConsumer component is placed inside the TestProvider
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully wrapped the App component with TestProvider, making the context available throughout your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the TestProvider wraps the entire App component content, including the TestConsumer.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not properly wrapped with TestProvider. Remember to wrap the entire component content with <TestProvider> tags.
